analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1990 tax increases on high earners, luxury goods, and other items.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced beyond a committee referral and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out the tax increases Congress passed in the 1990 budget deal, including the higher income tax rates on top earners, the new excise (sales) taxes on goods like luxury cars and boats, and the other revenue increases from that law. It was introduced by one House Republican with 16 Republican cosponsors and was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where it stayed. No committee action was ever taken and no vote was ever held in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households would gain the most, since the bill repeals the 1990 law's provisions "affecting high-income individuals" — the higher marginal tax rates on top earners. Makers and buyers of taxed luxury goods (yachts, cars, jewelry, furs, aircraft) would gain from the repeal of the new excise taxes, and drivers would gain from repeal of the 1990 gasoline tax increase. The cost would be lost federal revenue, borne as a larger deficit or as offsetting tax increases and spending cuts falling on other taxpayers and programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and luxury goods makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Part I of Subtitle A of the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1990, the provisions affecting high-income individuals, undoing the higher income tax rates imposed on top earners in the 1990 budget deal.
It repeals Subtitle B, the excise tax provisions, which under the 1990 law included new sales taxes on luxury goods and an increase in the gasoline tax.
It repeals Subtitle C, the 1990 law's remaining revenue increases, so the entire package of tax increases enacted in 1990 would be rolled back.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The 1990 tax increases were passed specifically to reduce the budget deficit; repealing them without replacement revenue would deepen the deficit, or require other tax increases and spending cuts elsewhere. Because the bill repeals the provisions aimed at high earners, the lost revenue is concentrated among the highest-income taxpayers, and the general public bears whatever deficit or offsetting burden results.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers, through deficits or offsets

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals revenue increases with nothing to replace them. The 1990 increases were enacted to shrink a large federal deficit; rolling them back would have added to the deficit or forced tax increases and spending cuts elsewhere in the code.

The largest benefit flows to high-income individuals, since the bill repeals the 1990 law's provisions 'affecting high-income individuals' — the provisions aimed at top tax rates. Lower- and middle-income taxpayers would see only the smaller excise-tax relief, such as the gasoline tax.

Repealing the excise taxes would remove revenue the 1990 law counted on, and the bill's text exempts only taxes already imposed before enactment, so the change would be mostly prospective rather than a refund.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles a modest, broadly felt benefit — repeal of excise taxes including the gasoline tax increase, which would slightly lower prices at the pump — with a large benefit aimed at the highest earners through repeal of the 1990 top-rate increases. The cost is unaddressed: the 1990 revenue was raised to cut the deficit, so repeal without offsets either deepens the deficit or shifts the burden to other taxpayers and programs. As written, the balance tilts toward the highest-income households.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1991, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and no action was ever taken on it; it died there when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. William Dannemeyer introduced H.R. 2257 on May 8, 1991, to repeal the tax increases contained in the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1990.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day it was introduced; that was the last action in its two-year history.
The bill would have repealed the 1990 law's provisions affecting high-income individuals, its excise tax subtitle, and its other revenue increases.
Sixteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
No committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the 1990 tax increases — including the higher rates on top earners — stayed in place, so general taxpayers and deficit reduction came out ahead relative to the bill's enactment; no one gained a legislative benefit from its failure, but the concentrated beneficiaries it would have created did not materialize.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Deficit reduction; top earners kept paying

for.name: Rep. William E. Dannemeyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 8, 1991 to repeal the 1990 tax increases; it was referred to Ways and Means.

for.name: 16 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to repeal the 1990 tax increases.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 8, 1991 and took no further action on it — no markup, no floor report — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill's largest effect is repealing the 1990 law's provisions affecting high-income individuals, cutting top marginal rates. The benefit concentrates among the wealthiest taxpayers while the offsetting deficit or replacement burden falls broadly.

industries.industry: Luxury goods manufacturers (boats, cars, jewelry, furs, aircraft)
industries.note: Repealing the 1990 excise taxes would lift the new luxury sales taxes, which depressed sales and cost jobs in boat building and similar trades after 1990. Producers and their workers would benefit directly.
The 1990 law raised the gasoline tax; the bill repeals the excise subtitle containing it, slightly lowering pump prices. This is the provision ordinary consumers would feel most.
The bill strips out revenue increases enacted specifically to reduce the 1990 deficit, deepening it unless offset by other tax increases or spending cuts.
